Overview

Basalt is a C++23 widget library. It follows the Cubit design system. Basalt turns a widget tree into paint commands and accessibility snapshots. Your application supplies the window, the renderer, and the input events.

This guide has four parts. This overview describes what Basalt does. The architecture chapter describes how the parts fit together. The getting-started chapter shows how to build a first program. The widgets chapter has one page for each widget.

Who this guide is for

This guide is for C++ programmers. You must know C++20 or later and CMake. You do not need to know Cubit, HarfBuzz, or any GUI library.

What Basalt does

Basalt does these tasks:

  • It keeps a tree of widgets and lays them out.
  • It routes input events to widgets and manages keyboard focus.
  • It records what to draw as a list of paint commands.
  • It shapes and lays out Unicode text, including bidirectional text and line breaks.
  • It builds a semantic tree for assistive technology.
  • It supplies Cubit colors, sizes, and text styles as a theme.

What Basalt does not do

Basalt does not do these tasks. Your application, called the host in this guide, does them.

  • It does not create windows.
  • It does not draw pixels. It gives your renderer a list of paint commands.
  • It does not read keyboard, mouse, or touch input from the operating system.
  • It does not talk to a platform accessibility API. It gives you a snapshot to send to one.
  • It does not open file dialogs. The host supplies a function that does.

This split makes Basalt portable. The same widget tree works with SDL and Skia, with a GPU renderer, or with a test that has no window.

Layers

The library has three layers.

Layer Contents
Core Geometry, units, color, theme, widget tree, layout, events, focus, accessibility, paint commands
Text Font discovery, fallback, shaping, bidirectional text, line breaking, paragraphs
Widgets Box, label, button, text field, menu, tabs, dialog, and the other Cubit widgets

The header basalt/basalt.h includes every public header.

Requirements

Basalt needs CMake 3.25 or later. It needs a C++23 compiler and standard library that support std::expected and <print>. The README.md file lists the tested compilers and the build options.

Architecture

Basalt has one central object, the widget tree. The host feeds events into it and reads paint commands out of it. This chapter describes each part and the order in which they run.

Host boundary

The host is your application. The host and Basalt exchange data in one loop.

The host does four jobs:

  1. It translates platform input into basalt::event values.
  2. It tells the tree the viewport size and the display scale.
  3. It runs the frame cycle when the tree asks for a frame.
  4. It draws the paint commands.

All positions in Basalt are layout pixels. A layout pixel is a window coordinate before the display scale. The renderer multiplies by the display scale to get device pixels.

Widget tree

A widget_tree owns the root widget of one window. It also holds the state that all widgets in that window share: the theme, the scale factors, keyboard focus, pending layout, and damage.

A widget is a node. It owns its children through std::unique_ptr. Because a parent owns its children, a tree has no cycles. Code that must refer to a widget from outside the tree uses a widget_id.

You make a custom widget by deriving from widget. You then override the hooks you need:

Hook Purpose
on_measure Report the size the widget wants.
on_layout Set the bounds of the children.
on_paint Record the widget’s drawing.
on_paint_overlay Record drawing that must appear above the children.
on_event Handle an event. Return true when the event is handled.
accessibility_info Describe the widget to assistive technology.
on_attached, on_detached React when the widget joins or leaves a tree.

A widget is detached, attaching, attached, or detaching. on_attached runs parent-first. on_detached runs children-first.

Frame cycle

The tree does not draw by itself. It asks the host for a frame, and the host runs the cycle.

  1. The tree calls the handler set with set_frame_request_handler. This happens once, when the tree goes from idle to needing a frame.
  2. The host calls advance_animations with a monotonic time.
  3. The host calls update_layout.
  4. The host calls take_damage. The result is the list of areas that need repaint. Taking the damage completes the frame request.
  5. The host calls paint_tree and draws the commands.
  6. The host calls collect_garbage. This destroys widgets that were removed with destroy_later.

needs_frame() reports whether the tree needs another frame. A host that polls can use it instead of the handler.

Layout

Layout has two passes. The first pass is measurement. The second pass is placement.

widget::measure returns the size that a widget wants within a set of constraints. The tree remembers the answer until layout is invalidated. Measurement must not change the tree.

widget::on_layout runs top-down. A container sets the bounds of each child with set_bounds. Changing a size marks the widget for layout, so the children of a resized widget are laid out in the same pass.

invalidate_layout marks a widget and all its ancestors. Widgets call it when their content changes. You rarely call it yourself.

Lengths use units. A fixed length scales with zoom. A relative length also scales with the user’s text-size preference. widget::resolve converts a length to layout pixels.

Painting

paint_tree walks the tree back to front and records paint_commands. A paint_commands value is a std::vector of a std::variant of command types:

  • fill and stroke commands for rectangles and rounded rectangles,
  • line commands,
  • glyph-run and image commands,
  • push and pop commands for clip, transform, and layer.

Widgets do not create commands directly. They call functions on render_context. Clip, transform, and layer calls return a scope object. The previous state returns when the scope is destroyed.

The host renderer reads the commands in order. A renderer needs one case for each command type. The Skia example in examples/common/skia_replay.cpp is a complete renderer.

To draw a glyph run, a renderer can load the font file from font_face::data() into its own font engine. It must then apply variation_weight() itself. A renderer without a font engine can use font_face::outline. It gives the outline of one glyph as a path, with the weight of the face applied.

Each widget paints inside its own bounds and its own coordinates. The tree clips children to the bounds of the parent. A disabled subtree is drawn in a layer at the theme’s disabled opacity.

Input and focus

An event is a std::variant of pointer, wheel, key, text input, IME, window, command, and file drop events. The host creates these values and passes them to event_router::dispatch.

The router sends pointer events to the widget under the pointer. It sends keyboard events to the focused widget. An event bubbles from the target up to the root until a widget returns true from on_event. The router skips disabled widgets.

The focus_manager of the tree tracks keyboard focus. A press focuses the innermost widget that accepts focus by click. An unhandled Tab moves focus to the next widget. Each widget has a focus_policy and a focus_scope.

Each widget has an interaction_state with the hover, press, and focus flags. Widgets read these flags when they paint.

The host must call router.update_hover() after layout. Widgets can move under a pointer that did not move.

Accessibility

A widget describes itself with accessibility_info. The call accessibility::build(tree) produces an immutable accessibility::tree. The tree contains nodes with a role, a name, a state, and a list of actions.

The snapshot does not refer to widgets. A platform bridge keeps one snapshot, builds the next one, and sends the difference to the platform. Basalt does not include a platform bridge.

Text

The text layer is in the basalt::text namespace. It has four parts.

Type Purpose
font_manager Finds fonts and chooses fallbacks. It reads only the fonts you add.
text_shaper Converts text to glyph runs with HarfBuzz.
paragraph and text_layout Break text into lines and lay out paragraphs.
bidi and line_break Implement the Unicode bidirectional and line-break algorithms.

HarfBuzz is a private dependency. No public header includes it.

The tree holds a pointer to a text_shaper. The host must keep the shaper alive for as long as the tree uses it. Without a shaper, text measures as zero width.

A text_shaper is not thread-safe. Shaping changes the scale of a font that all callers of the same font_manager share. Use one thread for each font_manager.

Theme

A theme holds the resolved Cubit tokens for one color scheme and one density. Create one with make_theme(color_scheme, density). Widgets read colors, sizes, and text styles from tree.theme(). Call tree.set_theme to change the theme. The change repaints the whole tree.

The raw token values are in generated/basalt/tokens.h. Do not edit this file. Regenerate it with just tokens.

Getting Started

This chapter builds a small program in seven steps. The program makes a widget tree with a label and a button, sends a click to the button, and records paint commands. It has no window, so it runs on any machine. The last section explains how to connect it to a window.

Step 1: Add Basalt to your project

Add Basalt with CMake FetchContent. Use a release tag as GIT_TAG.

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(hello LANGUAGES CXX)

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(basalt
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/nadiasvertex/basalt.git
  GIT_TAG v0.3.0)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(basalt)

add_executable(hello main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(hello PRIVATE basalt::basalt)

Basalt can also be used with add_subdirectory or find_package. See README.md for both. The build downloads HarfBuzz at configure time.

Step 2: Load fonts

Basalt does not search for fonts by itself. Add the fonts you want to a font_manager. Then create a text_shaper that uses it.

#include "basalt/basalt.h"

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <format>
#include <memory>
#include <print>
#include <string>

auto main(int argc, char **argv) -> int {
  if (argc < 2) {
    std::println(stderr, "usage: hello <font file>");
    return EXIT_FAILURE;
  }

  auto fonts = basalt::text::font_manager{};
  if (fonts.add_file(argv[1]) == 0) {
    std::println(stderr, "Cannot load the font {}", argv[1]);
    return EXIT_FAILURE;
  }
  auto const shaper = basalt::text::text_shaper{fonts};

add_file returns the number of faces that it added. Use add_system_fonts to add the fonts of the operating system. The font_manager must stay alive while the shaper is in use. Do not shape on two threads with the same font_manager at the same time.

Step 3: Create the widget tree

Make a widget_tree with a theme. Give it the shaper and the viewport size.

  auto tree = basalt::widget_tree{basalt::make_theme(basalt::color_scheme::light)};
  tree.set_text_shaper(&shaper);
  tree.set_viewport({480, 240});

The viewport is in layout pixels. In a real program, you set it from the window size. You also set the display scale with set_scale.

Step 4: Add widgets

Make a vertical box the root. Add a label and a button to it.

  auto clicks = 0;
  auto &root = tree.emplace_root<basalt::box>(basalt::axis::vertical);
  root.set_padding(basalt::length_insets::uniform(basalt::fixed(16)));
  root.set_gap(basalt::fixed(8));
  auto &status = root.emplace_child<basalt::label>("Clicks: 0");
  auto &press = root.emplace_child<basalt::button>("Count a click");
  press.set_variant(basalt::button_variant::primary);
  press.set_on_press([&] { status.set_text(std::format("Clicks: {}", ++clicks)); });

emplace_root and emplace_child construct the widget and return a reference to it. The tree owns the widgets. The references stay valid until you remove the widget.

Step 5: Make the event router

An event_router sends events to widgets in one tree. The router must not outlive the tree.

  auto router = basalt::event_router{tree};
  auto commands = basalt::paint_commands{};

Step 6: Run the frame cycle

Put the cycle in a function. Call it each time the tree needs a frame.

  auto const frame = [&] {
    tree.advance_animations(std::chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch());
    tree.update_layout();
    router.update_hover();
    auto const damage = tree.take_damage();
    if (!damage.empty()) {
      commands.clear();
      basalt::paint_tree(tree, commands);
    }
    tree.collect_garbage();
  };

The order is important. Layout must run before damage is taken. Damage must be taken before painting. See the frame cycle for the reason.

Step 7: Send input and read the result

Run one frame. Then send a pointer press and release to the center of the button. In a real program, the host translates window events into basalt::event values.

  frame();
  auto const center = press.bounds_in_root().center();
  for (auto const action : {basalt::pointer_action::down, basalt::pointer_action::up}) {
    router.dispatch(basalt::pointer_event{.action = action,
                                          .position = center,
                                          .button = basalt::pointer_button::primary});
  }
  frame();

  std::println("{} ({} paint commands)", status.text(), commands.size());
  return clicks == 1 ? EXIT_SUCCESS : EXIT_FAILURE;
}

Build and run the program with the path of a font file. For example, use a Noto Sans file from tests/data/fonts. The program prints Clicks: 1 and the number of paint commands.

Connect to a window

A program with a window has the same parts. These changes make it a full application:

  1. Create a window with your platform library.
  2. Translate each platform event into a basalt::event. Pass it to router.dispatch.
  3. On a resize or scale change, call tree.set_viewport and tree.set_scale.
  4. Call tree.set_frame_request_handler to wake the event loop. Run frame in the loop.
  5. Draw commands with your renderer, in order. Multiply layout pixels by the display scale.

The examples/sdl_skia directory has a complete host. Build and run it with just demo-sdl-skia. The first build compiles Skia, so it takes a long time.

Widgets

This chapter describes each widget in Basalt. Every page states what the widget is for, how to create and control it in code, and which events it reports. Every page also names a short example program in examples/widgets/ and shows a screenshot of its output. The pages follow the same order and use the same headings, so you can compare widgets quickly.

Common rules

All widgets follow these rules. The pages repeat a rule only when the widget changes it.

  • The tree owns every widget. Use emplace_root on the tree and emplace_child on a parent to create a widget. Both return a reference to the new widget. The reference stays valid until you remove the widget.
  • Most setters that you call from code do not call the change handler of the widget. Handlers run when the user, or assistive technology, changes the value. tab_bar::select is an exception, and its page says so.
  • A disabled widget ignores input. Call set_enabled(false) to disable a widget.
  • Each widget describes itself to assistive technology in accessibility_info(). Give controls that have no visible text an accessible name.
  • A widget that is not a child of an overlay_host cannot show popups. Menus, selects, popovers and dialogs need an overlay_host above them.

Run the examples

Each example is a small program without a window. It builds one widget, sends simulated input to it, and prints what the handlers received. The programs need CMake, Ninja, and the sources of Skia. Skia only draws the screenshot.

just widget-examples
.build/widgets/button

To write a screenshot, give the program a file name. The file uses the PAM format. The just screenshots recipe runs every program and converts the files to the PNG images in docs/images/widgets/. The conversion needs Python with Pillow.

.build/widgets/button button.pam

Examples use the example_host class from examples/widgets/common/. It makes a tree with fonts and a router, and it sends clicks, keys and text. A real program uses its own window system for this work, as examples/sdl_skia shows.

Widget list

Widget Purpose Classes
Accordion Sections that expand and collapse accordion, accordion_item
Avatar A person or entity as a photo or initials avatar
Box A row or column of children box
Button An action button

Chip A compact tag, filter or removable value chip, chip_group
Dialog A message with buttons dialog

Separator A line between groups separator

Stack Layers of children stack
Status bar Facts along the bottom of a window status_bar

Tooltip A short hint tooltip, tooltip_anchor
